In Bulli and Singleton, different types of geosynthetics (geogrid, geotextile and geocomposite) were installed to investigate their relative advantages in relation to various aperture sizes and types of subgrade. A key objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of these artificial inclusions on the vertical and lateral track deformation as the large-scale laboratory tests provided evidence that grids reduce particle breakage by restraining the movement of aggregates and by increasing the effective confining pressure such that excessive dilation is curtailed. The geogrids were more affective at controlling displacement when the track was constructed on a soft subgrade such as estuarine soil. With the tracks constructed directly onto estuarine planes consisting of the inevitable deep and saturated soft clay and silt deposits at Sandgate, prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs) were installed to a depth of less than 8 m to swiftly consolidate the soft upper clay stratum thereby helping resist long term track settlement while increasing the bearing capacity and shear strength. A sophisticated finite element program was developed to capture the behaviour of ballast, subballast and subgrade under cyclic loading via a coupled flow-deformation analysis capable of predicting the vertical and lateral displacement of the tracks, as well as the build-up of excess porewater pressure in the soft estuarine clay. The field data provided by the track owner (one year after the initial design and FEM predictions) proved that PVDs improved track stability by reducing the lateral movements of the subgrade while increasing its load bearing capacity. 1 Introduction In Australia, the rail transportation system plays a significant role in the conveyance of bulk freight and passengers. The rail track structure is categorised into two parts: (i) superstructure consisting of rail, fastening systems, and sleepers; and (ii) substructure consisting of ballast, capping, structural fill, and subgrade. The engineering behaviour of ballast is one of the most important aspects governing the stability and performance of a railway track because its progressive degradation under heavy cyclic loads applied by freight and passenger trains contributes largely to overall track deformation (Indraratna et al. 2011). In order to improve track performance and reduce the cost of maintenance, geosynthetic grids can be beneficial, and if waste ballast is cleaned, sieved, and then re-used in track reinforced with geosynthetics, it is also an economically feasible alternative. The use of geosynthetics for drainage and internal track confinement, as well as a separation layer between the ballast and subballast, is highly desirable (Raymond 2002; Brown et al. 2007; Indraratna et al. 2007; 2010a; 2010b; 2013; 2014b; 2014c). Both the type of reinforcement and its layout played a vital role in improving the performance of the track (Indraratna & Nimbalkar 2013). The results of large-scale tests clearly illustrated how shock mats (shock absorbing rubber mats) improved the performance of ballast subjected to impact blows (Nimbalkar et al. 2012) as well as number of cyclic load applications (Indraratna et al. 2014a). Evidence on long-term serviceability and maintenance

Geosynthetics improve long-term serviceability by reducing settlement and track irregularity, preserving track geometry, and extending maintenance intervals. The field trial evidence shows that geosynthetics can reduce lateral movements of the subgrade, increase load-bearing capacity, and resist long-term track settlement, especially when combined with prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs) on soft subgrades such as estuarine clay and silt [N3-F1]. This is important because soft soils are prone to progressive deterioration, densification, and loss of track geometry under cyclic loading, which leads to differential settlement and track deformation [N2-R4]. The use of geosynthetics therefore helps maintain more consistent track geometry over time, which is directly tied to reduced irregularity and improved serviceability [N3-F1].

On maintenance requirements and track geometry, the evidence suggests that geosynthetic use can reduce the frequency of track renewal and maintenance. The overview states that geosynthetics may significantly extend design life, reduce the time required to renew track, and reduce overall material costs [N4-F2]. This is consistent with the field trial findings that geosynthetics help preserve track stability and resist progressive deformation, which in turn reduces the need for frequent interventions [N3-F1]. The same source also notes that geosynthetics can help maintain track geometry by restraining particle movement, which reduces the risk of differential settlement and track irregularity [N3-F1]. Thus, track geometry is less likely to degrade rapidly when geosynthetics are used, and maintenance can be spaced farther apart.

The degradation or failure modes mitigated by geosynthetic use include progressive ballast degradation, excessive particle breakage, and the upward migration of fines from subballast and subgrade layers. The field trial evidence explicitly states that geogrids reduce particle breakage by restraining aggregate movement and increasing effective confining pressure, which curtails excessive dilation [N3-F1]. It also says that geocomposites stabilize recycled ballast much more effectively than geogrids and prevent ballast fouling due to upward fine migration [N3-F1]. Additionally, the overview notes that geosynthetics can prevent slurry formation at the ballast/subgrade interface, reduce pumping of fines into the ballast, and reduce the risk of differential settlements and unacceptable track deformations [N4-F2]. These mechanisms collectively mitigate the failure modes of ballast fouling, loss of drainage capacity, and progressive track settlement.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear long-term serviceability benefit: geosynthetics reduce settlement, preserve track geometry, lower maintenance demands, and mitigate the degradation processes that threaten track stability over time [N2-R4][N3-F1][N4-F2].

Technical mechanisms of performance improvement

Geosynthetics improve ballast performance by confining and stabilizing the ballast under traffic loading. The field trial evidence states that geogrids reduce particle breakage by restraining aggregate movement and increasing effective confining pressure, thereby curtailing excessive dilation [N3-F1]. It also says that geocomposites stabilize recycled ballast much more effectively than geogrids, which suggests that confinement and interlocking action are central to performance improvement [N3-F1]. The overview further explains that geosynthetics can enhance track performance by reducing the time required to renew track and by reducing maintenance costs, implying that they contribute to long-term stability rather than just short-term load response [N4-F2]. This is consistent with the idea that geosynthetics act as a structural reinforcement layer, limiting deformation and spreading of stresses under repeated loading.

Drainage and permeability improvements affect pore pressure and settlement. The overview notes that geosynthetics provide drainage, filtration, and separation functions, and that good drainage is critically important to avoid track deterioration due to water action from precipitation or from the subgrade into the ballast layers [N4-F2]. It specifically says that geosynthetics can be used to prevent pumping and slurry formation at the ballast/subgrade interface, which would otherwise increase pore pressures and reduce bearing capacity [N4-F2]. The field trial evidence similarly indicates that PVDs were used to consolidate soft upper clay strata, reduce porewater pressure, and resist long-term track settlement [N3-F1]. While the provided evidence does not give a full quantitative drainage-permeability model, it clearly links improved drainage with reduced pore-water pressure, reduced pumping, and lower settlement risk [N4-F2][N3-F1].

Shear resistance and frictional interaction improve lateral stability. The evidence states that geosynthetics can restrain movement of aggregates, increase effective confining pressure, and reduce lateral displacements [N3-F1]. It also notes that the use of geogrids can improve bearing capacity and shear strength in soft soils, and that the reinforcement layout plays a vital role in track performance [N3-F1]. The overview adds that geosynthetics provide separation, filtration, drainage, and stabilization functions, and that they help resist progressive shear failure and excessive plastic deformation [N4-F2]. These statements together show that shear resistance and frictional interaction are not just secondary effects but core mechanisms: they limit lateral spreading, prevent fines migration, and improve the ability of the ballast layer to sustain lateral loads without excessive deformation [N3-F1][N4-F2].

In summary, geosynthetics improve mechanical performance by confining the ballast, improving drainage to reduce pore pressure and settlement, and enhancing lateral stability through shear resistance and frictional interaction [N3-F1][N4-F2]. The evidence supports a multi-function mechanism rather than a single isolated benefit.

Design and implementation considerations

Typical geosynthetic placement and layering configurations are described as geotextiles, geogrids, geocomposites, and geocells installed within or beneath ballast and sub-ballast layers [N4-F2][N4-R1]. The overview also notes that geosynthetics may be placed directly on the soft subgrade, beneath the ballast, or within the ballast/sub-ballast layers [N4-F2]. The field trial evidence provides a concrete example: in Bulli and Singleton, different types of geosynthetics were installed to evaluate their relative advantages, with geogrids, geotextiles, and geocomposites used at the ballast-capping interface or in the track structure [N3-F1]. It also describes the use of prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs) in soft estuarine subgrades, which indicates that drainage systems are often integrated with geosynthetic placement to address soft-soil conditions [N3-F1]. Overall, the most common configuration is to use geosynthetics as a separation, filtration, drainage, or stabilization layer within the ballast or sub-ballast system, with specific placement depending on subgrade condition [N4-F2][N3-F1].

Important design parameters include thickness, spacing, and orientation. The overview emphasizes that the placement and layout of geosynthetics are important because they influence track performance and that the reinforcement layout played a vital role in improving track performance [N3-F1]. The field trial evidence similarly states that the relative performance of geosynthetics was evaluated by testing different aperture sizes and types of subgrade, and that the layout of the reinforcement mattered significantly [N3-F1]. The geosynthetic design standard also stresses that the design should fulfill the function of stabilization of granular layers, which implies that thickness and spacing must be chosen to provide adequate confining pressure and load transfer without excessive deformation [N5-R1]. While the provided evidence does not give a detailed quantitative design matrix, it clearly supports that spacing, orientation, and layout are design-critical factors that affect how well geosynthetics stabilize and confine the ballast [N3-F1][N5-R1].

Limitations and conditions where geosynthetics may not be optimal include soft, compressible, or highly permeable subgrades, as well as situations where drainage is inadequate or where excessive fines migration occurs. The field trial evidence explicitly says that geogrids were more effective at controlling displacement on soft subgrades such as estuarine soil, and that PVDs were used to consolidate soft clay and silt deposits [N3-F1]. The overview similarly states that geosynthetics may be used to reduce or replace traditional graded sub-ballast or sand blankets on soft soils, but that proper understanding of load transfer mechanisms is essential to minimize maintenance costs [N4-F2]. This implies that geosynthetics are especially useful where the underlying soil is weak and prone to settlement, but their value is conditional on proper design and installation rather than a universal solution [N3-F1][N4-F2]. The evidence does not explicitly list all possible limitations, but the repeated emphasis on subgrade condition, drainage, and reinforcement layout indicates that geosynthetics are not optimally suited to every geotechnical environment without careful design [N5-R1][N3-F1].

Field evidence and performance validation

Specific field test results and performance metrics are provided in the field trial evidence. In Bulli, NSW, a field trial was conducted on an instrumented railway track with a geocomposite installed at the ballast-capping interface. The relative performance of moderately graded recycled ballast compared to very uniform fresh ballast was also evaluated [N3-F1]. In Singleton, different types of geosynthetics were tested, including geogrids and geocomposites, to study their relative advantages [N3-F1]. At Sandgate, prefabricated vertical drains were installed to consolidate soft upper clay strata and reduce long-term track settlement [N3-F1]. These field trials are important because they go beyond laboratory studies and show that geosynthetic-enhanced track can be implemented in real-world conditions.

Comparison of geosynthetic-enhanced versus conventional ballast behavior is supported by the evidence that geogrids reduce particle breakage and excessive dilation, geocomposites stabilize recycled ballast more effectively than geogrids, and PVDs improve track stability by reducing lateral movements of the subgrade while increasing load-bearing capacity [N3-F1]. The overview also states that geosynthetics can reduce settlements associated with lateral spreading and that they can provide stabilization, drainage, filtration, and separation functions [N4-F2]. These comparisons suggest that geosynthetic-enhanced ballast layers behave more stably under cyclic loading and are less prone to progressive deformation than conventional ballast layers, especially when combined with drainage systems [N3-F1][N4-F2].

Any observed trade-offs or unexpected outcomes are limited in the provided evidence, but the field trial results do highlight a few important points. The study notes that the effectiveness of geosynthetics depends on subgrade condition and reinforcement layout, and that different aperture sizes and subgrade types were evaluated to find the best relative advantages [N3-F1]. It also implies that the choice between geogrids, geotextiles, and geocomposites matters because each type may perform differently under the same loading and subgrade conditions. The evidence also suggests that geosynthetics may not always eliminate the need for maintenance, because the track owner’s field data showed that PVDs improved track stability, but the paper still focuses on performance assessment rather than claiming a perfect solution [N3-F1]. Overall, the field evidence supports a practical conclusion: geosynthetics can improve performance, but their success depends on careful design, placement, and adaptation to local geotechnical conditions [N3-F1][N4-F2].

## Integrated synthesis of how geosynthetics enhance mechanical performance and long-term serviceability of railway ballast layers

Geosynthetics have been introduced into railway ballast systems to improve both the immediate mechanical response to traffic loading and the long-term serviceability of the track. The evidence from the branch reports points to a multi-function mechanism: geosynthetics confine and stabilize the ballast, improve drainage and pore-pressure control, and enhance lateral stability through shear resistance and frictional interaction. At the same time, they help reduce settlement, preserve track geometry, and extend maintenance intervals. The design and implementation considerations further show that placement, layering, spacing, orientation, and subgrade conditions are critical to realizing these benefits. Overall, geosynthetics are not a single isolated fix but a layered geotechnical intervention that addresses both the mechanical behavior and the service-life challenges of railway ballast layers.

---

## 1) How geosynthetics improve mechanical performance

### Confining and stabilizing ballast under traffic loading
The branch reports show that geosynthetics act as a confinement mechanism under traffic loading. The field trial evidence states that geogrids reduce particle breakage by restraining aggregate movement and increasing effective confining pressure, thereby curtailing excessive dilation [N3-F1]. It also says that geocomposites stabilize recycled ballast much more effectively than geogrids, indicating that confinement and interlocking action are central to performance improvement [N3-F1]. The overview further explains that geosynthetics can enhance track performance by reducing the time required to renew track and by reducing maintenance costs, implying that they contribute to long-term stability rather than just short-term load response [N4-F2]. This means that geosynthetics help the ballast layer resist deformation under repeated loading and spreading stresses.

### Drainage and permeability improvements affect pore pressure and settlement
A key mechanical benefit is the improvement in drainage and permeability. The overview notes that geosynthetics provide drainage, filtration, and separation functions, and that good drainage is critically important to avoid track deterioration due to water action from precipitation or from the subgrade into the ballast layers [N4-F2]. It specifically says that geosynthetics can be used to prevent pumping and slurry formation at the ballast/subgrade interface, which would otherwise increase pore pressures and reduce bearing capacity [N4-F2]. The field trial evidence similarly indicates that prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs) were used to consolidate soft upper clay strata, reduce porewater pressure, and resist long-term track settlement [N3-F1]. While the provided evidence does not give a full quantitative drainage-permeability model, it clearly links improved drainage with reduced pore-water pressure, reduced pumping, and lower settlement risk [N3-F1][N4-F2].

### Shear resistance and frictional interaction improve lateral stability
The evidence also shows that shear resistance and frictional interaction are important for lateral stability. The field trial evidence states that geogrids reduce particle breakage and excessive dilation, and that the reinforcement layout played a vital role in improving track performance [N3-F1]. The overview adds that geosynthetics help resist progressive shear failure and excessive plastic deformation [N4-F2]. This suggests that geosynthetics do not simply transmit loads but also limit lateral spreading and particle migration, thereby improving the lateral stability of the ballast layer under cyclic loading. The branch reports therefore support a multi-mode mechanism in which geosynthetics improve both vertical and lateral load transfer and deformation control.

---

## 2) How geosynthetics improve long-term serviceability

### Reducing settlement and track irregularity over time
The branch reports consistently indicate that geosynthetics reduce settlement and track irregularity. The field trial evidence notes that geogrids reduce particle breakage and excessive dilation, and that geocomposites stabilize recycled ballast much more effectively than geogrids [N3-F1]. It also says that PVDs improve track stability by reducing lateral movements of the subgrade while increasing load-bearing capacity and resisting long-term track settlement [N3-F1]. Geosynthetics therefore help counteract these progressive degradations by preserving track geometry and reducing differential settlement over time [N3-F1][N2-R4].

Geosynthetic use appears to reduce maintenance requirements and help preserve track geometry. This is consistent with the field trial findings that geosynthetics help preserve track stability and resist progressive deformation, which in turn reduces the need for frequent interventions [N3-F1].
